solutions.check: 32 entries verified against the grid (lengths, crossings, linked-clue mapping)

clue.text: Newspaper worker revives fabrication — troublemaker!

parts.note: a sub is a sub-editor, who checks and trims copy at a newspaper

indicators.note: a fabrication is something made up, so the letters of revives are made up into a new word

explanation.surface: A journalist brings back invented stories, stirring up trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: A sub is a sub-editor. 'Fabrication' suggests fake news in the surface, but it is the signal to rebuild the following word.
explanation.definitionFit: A subversive is a person who seeks to undermine an established system, a stirrer of trouble.

clue.text: Drugs up escort to relax

indicators.note: in a down clue, 'up' sends the letters upward, so they read backwards

parts.note: E is ecstasy, so drugs are Es
to escort someone out is to date them

explanation.surface: Someone takes drugs to unwind before a night with an escort.
explanation.walkthrough: SEDATE here is the verb, to calm someone down; 'to' just ties the definition to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: To sedate someone is to make them relax, usually with a drug.

clue.text: Raab's ultimate downfall? Gesture "Excellent idea!"

indicators.note: the ultimate letter is the last one

parts.note: rain is a fall coming down
a wave is a hand gesture

explanation.surface: Dominic Raab, the British Conservative politician, faces his downfall while someone gestures that it's a great idea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Downfall' reads as ruin, but split it: a fall from above, which is RAIN.
explanation.definitionFit: The answer is an exclamation of praise turned noun: a brainwave is the sudden flash of inspiration that deserves the cry.

clue.text: Capitalise on trumped-up top lie about vote

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the reworked letters go round the mark for a vote
trumped-up means invented or falsified, so the letters of top lie are concocted into a new order

parts.note: X is the cross a voter marks on a ballot paper

explanation.surface: A politician cashes in on a big falsehood told around election time, with a nod to Trump.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trumped-up' rearranges TOP LIE into EPLOIT, which goes 'about' X, the voting cross, after its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To exploit something is to make full use of it for profit, to capitalise on it.

clue.text: Endorsement: 'Contains nuts'

indicators.note: nuts means crazy, so the letters of CONTAINS go wild

explanation.surface: A food label bearing the allergy warning 'Contains nuts' as its seal of approval.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as an allergy warning on a packet; 'nuts' is really the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: sanction as a noun has the positive sense of official approval, the opposite of its penalty sense.

clue.text: Electorate very sore about Tory leader getting in

indicators.note: getting in means entering, so that letter goes inside the rearranged letters
about here means moved around, so the letters of sore are rearranged
a leader comes first, so only the opening letter of Tory is used

parts.note: only its first letter is used

explanation.surface: The voters are furious that the Conservative leader has won office.
explanation.walkthrough: V (very), then 'about' rearranges SORE into ORES, with T ('Tory leader') 'getting in' after the O.
explanation.definitionFit: The electorate is the whole body of people entitled to vote in an election.

clue.text: (& 30ac.) They've been driven more than once to break addicts with drug control agency initiatives

definitions.text: They've been driven more than once

indicators.note: to break into a word is to split it, so the initials go into the middle of the word for addicts
initiatives is read as initials, the first letter of each of the three words

parts.note: each of these three words gives up its opening letter

explanation.surface: A drugs agency launches schemes to get addicts off their habit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Initiatives' is read as initials. 'Driven' is the motoring sense, not motivated, and 'more than once' means by several owners.
explanation.definitionFit: Second-hand vehicles have had previous owners, so they have been driven by more than one person.

clue.text: Girl's brief victory against love — round of applause!

parts.note: Sal is a girl's name, short for Sally
V is the short form of victory, as in V-sign
love is nil in tennis, the shape of O

explanation.surface: A girl wins briefly against a lover, and the crowd applauds.
explanation.walkthrough: Sal is a common short form of Sally, and a salvo is literally a burst of gunfire, used figuratively for a burst of clapping.
explanation.definitionFit: A salvo of applause is a sudden burst of it, like a round.

clue.text: Leftover chow for a chow?

definitions.meaning: chow is slang for food, so this is uneaten food from a meal
a chow is also a dog breed, the chow chow, which takes the food home

explanation.surface: Scraps from dinner saved for the family dog.
explanation.walkthrough: The joke is the two chows: food, then a chow chow, a breed of dog. A doggy bag is supposedly for the dog.
explanation.definitionFit: A doggy bag holds a diner's uneaten food to take home, notionally for the dog.

clue.text: One member Rishi edges out — "disrespectful!"

parts.note: RISHI without its outer R and I

explanation.surface: An MP is thrown out by Rishi Sunak, the former British prime minister, and complains of disrespect.
explanation.walkthrough: Rishi is Rishi Sunak; 'edges out' reads as pushing someone aside but here strips the edge letters off his name.
explanation.definitionFit: Impish behaviour is cheekily mischievous, lacking due respect.

clue.text: Expressionless and insensitive, taking pot

explanation.surface: A blank-faced, unfeeling person helping themselves to the pot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pot' may suggest cannabis or a poker kitty; here it is simply a pan.
explanation.definitionFit: A deadpan face shows no expression.

clue.text: What jailbird does to 'bring up rear' in interval

parts.note: to lag is to trail behind

explanation.surface: A convict's routine in jail, with a hint of something nastier in 'bring up rear'.
explanation.walkthrough: The jailbird suggests LAG, slang for a convict, but LAG comes from 'bring up rear' instead; the jailbird supplies TIME.
explanation.definitionFit: A time lag is an interval between one event and another.

clue.text: Argentinian export makes Brown quit

explanation.surface: An Argentinian export forces Gordon Brown, the former British prime minister, to quit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Makes' is only a link word; the surface has Brown quitting, but BROWN and QUIT each give their own letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The tango is a dance from Argentina, exported worldwide.

clue.text: Dependency of "dismal trier" politician

indicators.note: something dismal is in a poor state, so the letters of trier are muddled

parts.note: a Tory is a member of the British Conservative Party

explanation.surface: A Conservative MP is mocked as a hopeless trier who depends on others.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dismal' rearranges TRIER into TERRI, then TORY, a British Conservative.
explanation.definitionFit: A dependency is a territory ruled by another country rather than being fully independent.

clue.text: Splinter group subdivision chucks out Labour's right wing

indicators.note: chucks out means throws away, so one letter is removed from the word for subdivision

parts.note: a fraction is a part or subdivision of a whole

indicators.note: the right wing of a word is its right-hand end, its last letter

parts.note: the possessive points to the word Labour, of which only the final letter is used

explanation.surface: A breakaway group inside the Labour Party expels the party's right-wingers.
explanation.walkthrough: The right wing of LABOUR is its last letter R, which 'chucks out' drops from FRACTION. The surface suggests party politics, where Labour is Britain's main left-of-centre party.
explanation.definitionFit: A faction is a small dissenting group within a larger party, a splinter group.

clue.text: "Dread pub, old boy," I start to admit

parts.note: PH is the map abbreviation for public house

indicators.note: the start of 'admit' is its first letter

parts.note: abbreviation for old boy, a former pupil

explanation.surface: An old man confesses he dreads going to the pub.
explanation.walkthrough: PH for pub is found on British Ordnance Survey maps; OB, an old boy, is a former pupil of a school.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a phobia is an extreme, irrational fear of something.

clue.text: Barney boobs — virtually a feature of the campaign trail

definitions.text: a feature of the campaign trail

parts.note: a barney is a row or fight
BUST, a bosom, without its last letter

explanation.surface: An election row over gaffes, the kind of thing that dogs a campaign.
explanation.walkthrough: A barney is British slang for a noisy quarrel. 'Boobs' reads as blunders but is BUST, a bosom.
explanation.definitionFit: A battle bus is the coach a party leader tours the country in during an election campaign.

clue.text: After lost deposit, Conservative becomes Trump-like?

indicators.note: after places the Conservative's letter behind the rearranged letters
lost means astray, so the letters of deposit wander into a new order

explanation.surface: A Tory candidate who loses his election deposit turns into a Trump imitator.
explanation.walkthrough: In UK elections a candidate with too few votes forfeits a cash deposit, which is the picture; 'lost' is really the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Despotic means ruling like a tyrant, and the question mark admits the jibe at Trump.

clue.text: Ex-PM takes hard look: result of stress and worry?

parts.note: Earl Grey, prime minister in the 1830s
H is hard, as on pencils
an air is a look or manner

explanation.surface: A former prime minister takes a hard look at the toll of office.
explanation.walkthrough: The ex-PM is Earl Grey, of the tea, rather than anyone recent.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom: worry is proverbially said to turn a person grey, hence the question mark.

clue.text: Issue of Farage finally getting team together

indicators.note: the final letter of FARAGE

parts.note: to merge is to join up as one team

explanation.surface: Nigel Farage, the Reform UK leader, has a problem assembling a team.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Issue' looks like a noun, a problem, but it is the verb: to come out.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the verb sense: to issue forth is to come out.

clue.text: Sex inside a rug, possibly a rock star's thing?

indicators.note: inside puts the word for sex within the rearranged letters
possibly signals that a rug can be read as another arrangement of the same letters

parts.note: it is an old euphemism for sex appeal or sex

explanation.surface: A rock star's antics on a rug, hinting at sex.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It' as a word for sex, or sex appeal, is an old euphemism; the question mark flags the loose definition of the star's instrument.
explanation.definitionFit: The electric guitar is the instrument most associated with a rock musician.

clue.text: Will confirmed as authentic degenerate on quitting

explanation.surface: A will is proved valid despite a wastrel heir walking away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Will' reads as a name or verb, but it is the legal document, and the whole phrase defines PROBATE.
explanation.definitionFit: Probate is the legal proving of a will as genuine.

clue.text: Puncture Cummings' weariness?

parts.note: to bore is to drill a hole
Dominic Cummings, Boris Johnson's adviser, known as Dom

explanation.surface: Deflating Dominic Cummings, the British political adviser, and his tiredness.
explanation.walkthrough: Cummings is Dominic Cummings, the former adviser to Boris Johnson; 'Puncture' is a verb here, to bore through.
explanation.definitionFit: Boredom is a weary lack of interest.

clue.text: Aborted ascent on an unknown peak

indicators.note: in a down clue, the first part sits on top of the rest

explanation.surface: A failed attempt on an unclimbed mountain.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'on' puts CLIM above A and X; the surface sounds like mountaineering, and CLIMAX is the peak it never reached.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the climax of a story or event is its highest point.

clue.text: Lawyers? They're pants!

definitions.meaning: a brief is slang for a barrister
pants as underwear, the close-fitting kind

explanation.surface: A sneer that lawyers are rubbish.
explanation.walkthrough: In British slang 'pants' means rubbish, which makes the surface an insult; it also means underpants.
explanation.definitionFit: A brief is slang for a lawyer; briefs are close-fitting pants.

clue.text: Somewhat crappy play about rigged trial

indicators.note: about means around, so one set of reworked letters surrounds the other
crappy means shoddily made, so the letters of play are knocked into a new order
rigged means fixed or tampered with, so the letters of trial are fiddled into a new order

explanation.surface: A review dismisses a poor courtroom drama about a fixed trial.
explanation.walkthrough: Both words are anagrammed: 'crappy' works on play and 'rigged' on trial, and the first set of letters goes round the second. 'Somewhat' is the definition, not a qualifier.
explanation.definitionFit: Partially means to some extent, not wholly, the same as somewhat.

clue.text: Who will scrape up the mess of profligate Republican?

definitions.text: Who will scrape up the mess

parts.note: a rake is a dissolute man
R is the abbreviation for Republican

explanation.surface: Who will clean up after a dissolute Republican?
explanation.walkthrough: The surface asks who cleans up a politician's scandals; the literal answer is whoever wields the rake.
explanation.definitionFit: A raker is one who rakes, scraping up debris.

clue.text: Straight strip, guv?

definitions.meaning: a strip for drawing straight lines
guv, short for governor, one who rules

explanation.surface: A cockney tells the boss to strip right off.
explanation.walkthrough: Guv is British slang for boss or governor, which the question mark stretches to a ruler.
explanation.definitionFit: A ruler is a straight measuring strip, and also someone who governs.

clue.text: Be prepared to fire Mike at a review

indicators.note: a review looks at the letters again, reordering them

explanation.surface: An employee is warned he may be sacked at his appraisal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fire' reads as sacking Mike at his review; the definition is about a gun.
explanation.definitionFit: To take aim is to line up a weapon ready to fire.

clue.text: Baldie beaten up outside university, likely to be picked up by ears

definitions.text: likely to be picked up by ears

indicators.note: outside means the scrambled letters sit around the letter for university
beaten up means knocked about, so the letters of Baldie are scrambled

explanation.surface: A bald man is assaulted near a university, loudly enough to be overheard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beaten up' rearranges BALDIE into ADIBLE, which goes 'outside' U (university) after its A.
explanation.definitionFit: Audible means loud enough to be heard, so a sound like that is caught by the ears.

clue.text: see 6ac.
Test REM with six free radicals

indicators.note: the letters are set free to rearrange

explanation.surface: A sleep lab tests REM sleep in six subjects, measuring free radicals.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Free radicals' is a chemistry phrase, but 'free' is the anagram signal and 'radicals' alone the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Radicals are people with extreme views, extremists.
